topic: JVM Internals (Memory Model, G1/ZGC, Class Loading)

questions.question: What is the primary cause of the `Metaspace` memory leak in this code?
options: A) `beanFactory.autowireBean(ruleInstance)` registers the instance in Spring internal lifecycle caches, retaining a strong reference to `ruleInstance`, which prevents `CustomClassLoader` and its loaded metadata from being garbage collected.
B) The `CustomClassLoader` uses `getClass().getClassLoader()` as its parent class loader, forcing all dynamically generated classes into the Bootstrap ClassLoader Metaspace region.
C) Dynamic byte code instantiation via `newInstance()` bypasses Garbage Collection unless `loader.finalize()` is manually invoked before `executeCustomRule` finishes.
D) Spring `@Service` singletons acquire a thread-level lock on `loader.defineClass()`, holding class metadata permanently in the JVM PermGen space.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) `beanFactory.autowireBean(ruleInstance)` registers the instance in Spring internal lifecycle caches, retaining a strong reference to `ruleInstance`, which prevents `CustomClassLoader` and its loaded metadata from being garbage collected.
questions.explanation: A Java `Class` can only be unloaded from `Metaspace` if its defining `ClassLoader` is eligible for Garbage Collection. A `ClassLoader` cannot be GC'd if any `Class` defined by it has live instances on the Heap. When `beanFactory.autowireBean(ruleInstance)` is called, Spring registers the object instance into internal lifecycle management pools (such as destruction/disposal caches). Because Spring maintains a strong reference to `ruleInstance`, `ruleInstance` keeps its `Class` alive, which in turn keeps `CustomClassLoader` alive, completely preventing `Metaspace` class unloading across executions.

questions.scenario: You are debugging a production issue where a low-latency microservice running on JDK 17 with ZGC (`-XX:+UseZGC`) experiences sudden, multi-second latency spikes under peak throughput. Inspection of GC logs reveals frequent `Allocation Stall` entries immediately preceding the application pauses. The JVM heap is fixed at `-Xms32g -Xmx32g`.
questions.question: What is the root cause of these `Allocation Stall` events under ZGC, and what is the appropriate fix?
options: A) The application is allocating memory at a higher rate than ZGC can reclaim it concurrently, forcing mutator threads to stall while waiting for GC cycles to complete; fix by tuning `-XX:ZAllocationSpikeTolerance` or increasing `-XX:ConcGCThreads`.
B) ZGC's colored pointers fail when heap usage exceeds 16GB, causing a full Stop-The-World compaction fallback; fix by setting `-XX:+UseCompressedOops`.
C) Metaspace expansion triggers a mandatory synchronous STW collection under ZGC; fix by pre-allocating `-XX:MetaspaceSize=2g`.
D) Thread Local Allocation Buffers (`TLABs`) are disabled by default under ZGC; fix by explicitly enabling `-XX:+UseTLAB`.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) The application is allocating memory at a higher rate than ZGC can reclaim it concurrently, forcing mutator threads to stall while waiting for GC cycles to complete; fix by tuning `-XX:ZAllocationSpikeTolerance` or increasing `-XX:ConcGCThreads`.
questions.explanation: ZGC is a concurrent garbage collector designed to keep STW pauses under 1 millisecond. However, if mutator application threads allocate memory faster than ZGC's concurrent marking and relocating phases can free memory, the heap becomes exhausted. When this happens, ZGC stalls the allocating application threads (`Allocation Stall`) until memory becomes available. Resolving this requires giving ZGC more CPU resources to finish GC phases faster by increasing `-XX:ConcGCThreads` or initiating GC earlier using `-XX:ZAllocationSpikeTolerance`.

questions.question: From a Java Memory Model (JMM) perspective, why does `processLoop()` continue running indefinitely after `shutdown()` is invoked by another thread?
options: A) Without `volatile` or explicit synchronization, the JMM allows CPU core caches to keep stale reads of `active`, and JIT (C2) optimizations can hoist `active` out of the loop into a single check (`hoisting`).
B) Spring `@Component` proxies generate thread-local shadow copies of instance fields, making field state mutations invisible across threads.
C) Non-volatile boolean writes in 64-bit HotSpot JVMs are non-atomic and lead to word tearing across CPU socket boundaries.
D) Spring Transaction Manager injects a `StoreLoad` memory barrier that prevents non-transactional methods like `processLoop()` from reading heap memory.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) Without `volatile` or explicit synchronization, the JMM allows CPU core caches to keep stale reads of `active`, and JIT (C2) optimizations can hoist `active` out of the loop into a single check (`hoisting`).
questions.explanation: According to the Java Memory Model (JMM), reads and writes to non-volatile fields do not establish a Happens-Before relationship. Without declaring `active` as `volatile` or accessing it via `synchronized`/locks, changes made by one thread in its CPU core cache are not guaranteed to be flushed to main memory or visible to other threads. Furthermore, the C2 JIT compiler optimizes `while (active)` into `if (active) { while(true) {} }` (loop hoisting) because it assumes `active` is not modified inside the local thread context.
